newsitem.title: SWEDEN: EU nations gain market share in arms exports-SIPRI.
newsitem.headline: EU nations gain market share in arms exports-SIPRI.

text.p: European Union countries have raised their market share of arms exports over the past decade but the United States is still the largest supplier, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute(SIPRI) said on Thursday.

European countries increased their market share of the global arms trade to about 28 percent last year from around 15 percent in 1987, said Siemon Wezeman, a researcher for the Swedish defence research organisation.
The U.S. market share is 44 percent compared to about 30 percent 10 years ago.
Meanwhile the worldwide arms trade has fallen by about half because of the end of the Cold War, Wezeman said as SIPRI released its 1997 yearbook.

"Eastern Europe has no money and no reason to buy anything. Western Europe is in the process of restructuring their armed forces but we could expect to see new orders in about five years," Wezeman told Reuters.
The fall in orders from western European countries is also because of changes in countries' defence needs, he said.
"Previously the countries pointed at a European war scenario. Now they are looking for another scenario, such as peacekeeping. For that you need very different kind of weapons," Wezeman said.
SIPRI said in its annual yearbook that the value of trade of conventional weapons was about the same last year as in 1995, at $22.98 billion, compared to $23.19 billion a year earlier.
After the United States, Russia was the second largest supplier of major conventional weapons with a 20 percent share of total deliveries.
France was the third largest supplier at nine percent, an increase from the previous year, because of deliveries to Taiwan within existing contracts.
Ukraine has emerged among former Soviet republics as an important exporter of arms, SIPRI said.
Ukraine inherited major missile production plants and significant capabilities to design and manufacture transport aircraft and armed vehicles.
Its arms exports rose to $100 million in 1995 from $28 million in 1993, and national export procedures have been rejigged to better organise arms export activity, SIPRI said.
SIPRI said that among importers, the data for 1996 tended to reinforce the main trends identified in 1995.
Three regions -- Asia, Europe and the Middle East -- remained the predominant centres of demand for imported weapons.
Total demand was still heavily concentrated in North America and Western Europe.
China, South Korea and Taiwan accounted for 30 percent of imports, and Asia in general for 50 percent, SIPRI said.
Middle Eastern countries import about 25 percent and European countries less than 20 percent.
Ten years ago imports were equally divided among Asia, Europe and the Middle East, with each region importing roughly about 30 percent.
Asia is a market rising because of increased wealth in the region, the modernisation of armed forces and the existence of several troubled spots.
"What we see now is still the beginning of major increases," Wezeman said.
